implementation_notes: Lea's original Java realization is a synchronized method that reads the state field, returns immediately when the state forbids the action, and only otherwise performs the check-and-transition - because both run under the same monitor, competing threads observe a consistent state and at most one proceeds. java.util.concurrent adds ready-made non-blocking attempts whose Try*/offer operations fail instead of waiting (ReentrantLock.tryLock(), Semaphore.tryAcquire(), BlockingQueue.offer(e)); use those when the guarded resource is already a lock, permit pool or queue, and keep the synchronized guard for bespoke object state. Either way the guarded state must be read and written under the same synchronization.
pitfalls: The state field must be read and written under the same monitor; a cached local, or a field read outside the monitor, can make threads balk forever on a stale state.
A balking method must not be called re-entrantly expecting progress: the monitor is reentrant, so a nested call sees the state the outer call just changed and silently does nothing.
Returning void hides refusals - callers cannot distinguish 'executed' from 'ignored' unless the method returns a boolean or status.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent try-attempts (non-blocking)
variants.implementation_notes: The library realization: java.util.concurrent classes offer fail-immediately twins of their blocking operations - ReentrantLock.tryLock() acquires only if the lock is free and otherwise returns false, BlockingQueue.offer(e) inserts only when space is immediately available (where put(e) blocks), Semaphore.tryAcquire() takes a permit only if one is free - and ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent performs the guarded one-winner update without an explicit lock. Bind this variant when the guarded resource already is one of those primitives or when blocking a request thread is unacceptable; note that tryLock() deliberately ignores a fair lock's ordering, so do not mix it with fairness requirements.
pitfalls: tryLock on a fair lock barges ahead of queued waiters (the javadoc says it does not honour fairness), so fairness guarantees are lost the moment the pattern is applied.
unlock() must run only after a successful tryLock(); calling it on the false branch throws IllegalMonitorStateException and hides the real flow.
The boolean results of offer/tryAcquire are easy to discard, after which a rejected operation looks exactly like a successful one.
